sectionsContent.title: Net Force from Free-Body Diagrams

items: A free-body diagram shows the object as a box with one labelled arrow per force, and no arrow for motion (S3.2). Balanced forces add to zero (S3.1).
A vector splits into x- and y-components (S2.1), and vectors add axis by axis (S2.2). Your calculator's tan⁻¹ only gives angles between −90° and 90°, so check the quadrant.

sectionsContent.directions: Work each problem in your notebook. Draw a free-body diagram, then find the net force. Give ∑F with a unit and a direction. Angles are measured from the x-axis: above or below +x, or above or below −x.

questions.prompt: Two movers slide a couch across the living room toward the front door. One pushes with 140 N and the other with 110 N, both toward the door. Friction from the carpet is 205 N. Take toward the door as positive. Find the net force on the couch.
questions.solution: + = toward the door. ∑F = 140 + 110 − 205 = 45 N. ∑F = 45 N toward the door.

steps.say: F_{N} and F_{g} balance. Their size is not given, so they are drawn equal.

partHeading: Part 1 · Net force in one dimension
Each problem names the positive direction. Weight and the normal force balance, so add the sideways forces with their signs.

questions.prompt: Your car stalls a block from the gas station. Two friends push it toward the station with 345 N and 310 N. Rolling friction on the tires is 185 N, and a headwind pushes back on the car with 60 N. Take toward the station as positive. Find the net force on the car.
questions.solution: + = toward the station. ∑F = 345 + 310 − 185 − 60 = 410 N. ∑F = 410 N toward the station.

steps.say: Both friction and the wind point back, so both are negative. F_{N} and F_{g} are not to scale: a car's weight is far larger.

questions.prompt: A dresser sits in the middle of a bedroom. Dad pushes it toward the window with 260 N. His son, on the other side, pushes it toward the door with 95 N. Friction from the floor is 165 N, toward the door. Take toward the window as positive. Find the net force on the dresser. Does the dresser start moving?
questions.solution: + = toward the window. ∑F = 260 − 95 − 165 = 0 N. The forces are balanced, so the dresser stays at rest. It does not start moving.
questions.finalAnswer: 0 N; the dresser does not start moving

steps.say: Balanced forces: it stays at rest. It does not start moving.

questions.prompt: Two kids pull a loaded wagon down the sidewalk, one with 36.0 N and one with 28.5 N, both forward. Friction on the wheels is 22.5 N. Near the street, their dad grabs the back of the wagon and pulls backward with 50.0 N. Take forward as positive.
parts: a.  Find the net force on the wagon.
b.  The wagon is still rolling forward at this moment. Explain how it can roll forward while the net force points backward.
questions.solution:
a. + = forward. ∑F = 36.0 + 28.5 − 22.5 − 50.0 = −8.0 N. ∑F = 8.0 N backward.
b. Net force changes the motion; it does not have to point the way the object moves. A backward net force on a wagon rolling forward slows it down. It keeps rolling forward until it stops.
questions.finalAnswer: a. 8.0 N backward (−8.0 N). b. A backward net force slows the wagon; it does not have to point the way it moves.

steps.say: b. Net force changes motion. A backward net force on a wagon rolling forward slows it down. It rolls forward until it stops.
Misconception to watch for: a moving object must have a net force pointing the way it moves.

questions.prompt: You pull a rolling suitcase through the airport at a steady speed with 40.0 N along the handle, 50.0° above +x. Find the x- and y-components of your pull.

steps.say: Weight is not given. F_{N} is drawn shorter than F_{g} because the pull lifts a little.

partHeading: +x points the way the object moves and +y points up. Find the x- and y-components first. The object stays on the ground, so the net force is the net horizontal force.

questions.prompt: A parent pushes a stroller with 65.0 N along the handle, 40.0° below +x. Rolling friction is 42.0 N. Find the components of the push, then the net force on the stroller with its direction.

steps.say: Only F_{x} moves the stroller forward. F_{y} pushes it into the ground.

questions.prompt: Maya drags a rolling cooler to the beach. She pulls 50.0 N on the handle at 60.0° above +x, and friction is 22.0 N. Her friend tells her to lower the handle to 20.0° above +x and pull just as hard.
parts: a.  Find the net force on the cooler for each angle.
b.  Which angle gives the larger net force? Use the components to say where the rest of her 50.0 N goes.
questions.solution:
a. 60.0°: Fx = 50.0 cos 60.0° = 25.0 N; ∑Fx = 25.0 − 22.0 = 3.0 N (+x). 20.0°: Fx = 50.0 cos 20.0° = 47.0 N; ∑Fx = 47.0 − 22.0 = 25.0 N (+x).
b. 20.0° gives the larger net force. At 60.0° most of the pull is vertical (Fy = 43.3 N), which lifts on the cooler instead of moving it forward. At 20.0°, Fy is only 17.1 N.
questions.finalAnswer: 60.0°: 3.0 N (+x); 20.0°: 25.0 N (+x). The lower handle wins.

steps.say: b. 20.0° wins. At 60.0° most of the pull is vertical (F_{y} = 43.3 N) and lifts the cooler. At 20.0°, F_{y} is only 17.1 N.

questions.prompt: A 15.0 kg wagon of firewood is pulled across a level driveway with 90.0 N along the handle, 35.0° above +x. Friction is 50.0 N.
parts: a.  Find the wagon's weight and the vertical component of the pull.
b.  Find the normal force on the wagon. Is it equal to the weight?
c.  Find the net force on the wagon with its direction.
questions.solution:
a. Fg = 15.0 × 9.8 = 147 N down. Fy = 90.0 sin 35.0° = 51.6 N up.
b. Vertical forces balance: FN + Fy = Fg, so FN = 147 − 51.6 = 95.4 N up. It is less than the weight, because the handle lifts part of the load.
c. Fx = 90.0 cos 35.0° = 73.7 N. ∑Fx = 73.7 − 50.0 = 23.7 N. ∑F = 23.7 N in the +x direction.
questions.finalAnswer: Fg = 147 N, Fy = 51.6 N; FN = 95.4 N (less than Fg); ∑F = 23.7 N in the +x direction

questions.prompt: Two cousins pull a sled across a frozen pond. One pulls 80.0 N along +x. The other pulls 35.0 N along +y. Find the net force on the sled.
partHeading: Part 3 · Two or more angled forces
Top views: +x points right, +y points up the page. Weight and the normal force cancel out of the page, so leave them off.

questions.prompt: Two friends pull a kayak across the sand. Jordan pulls 155 N at 40.0° above −x. Ava pulls 90.0 N at 70.0° above +x. Find the net force on the kayak. Check the quadrant before you give the angle.
questions.solution: Jordan: x = −155 cos 40.0° = −118.7 N, y = 155 sin 40.0° = 99.6 N. Ava: x = 90.0 cos 70.0° = 30.8 N, y = 90.0 sin 70.0° = 84.6 N. ∑Fx = −88.0 N, ∑Fy = 184.2 N. ∑F = √(88.0² + 184.2²) = 204 N. θ = tan⁻¹(184.2/88.0) = 64.5°. ∑Fx is negative and ∑Fy positive, so the net force is in the upper left: 204 N at 64.5° above −x.

steps.say: x negative, y positive: upper left, so the angle is measured from −x.

questions.prompt: Two movers drag a heavy box across a warehouse floor with two straps. Each pulls 85.0 N, one at 35.0° above +x and one at 35.0° below +x.
parts: a.  Find the net force the straps exert on the box.
b.  Find the net force if both movers pulled straight along +x.
c.  Do the two angled pulls give more or less net force than pulling straight? Use the components to explain why.
questions.solution:
a. ∑Fx = 2 × 85.0 cos 35.0° = 139 N. ∑Fy = 85.0 sin 35.0° − 85.0 sin 35.0° = 0. ∑F = 139 N along +x.
b. 85.0 + 85.0 = 170 N along +x.
c. Less. Only the x-components move the box forward. The y-components (48.8 N each) point opposite ways and cancel, so that part of each pull does nothing to move the box.
questions.finalAnswer: a. 139 N along +x. b. 170 N along +x. c. Less; the y-components cancel.

steps.say: c. Less. Only the x-components move the box. The y-components (48.8 N each) cancel each other.

questions.prompt: Sam is walking two dogs when both spot a squirrel. Max pulls his leash with 80.0 N at 30.0° above +x. Bella pulls hers with 75.0 N at 55.0° below +x. Sam plants his feet and does not move.
parts: a.  Find the net force the two leashes exert on Sam.
b.  Sam stays at rest. Find the force the ground must exert on his shoes, with its direction.
questions.solution:
a. ∑Fx = 80.0 cos 30.0° + 75.0 cos 55.0° = 69.3 + 43.0 = 112.3 N. ∑Fy = 80.0 sin 30.0° − 75.0 sin 55.0° = 40.0 − 61.4 = −21.4 N. ∑F = √(112.3² + 21.4²) = 114 N. θ = tan⁻¹(21.4/112.3) = 10.8°, below +x because ∑Fy is negative. Leashes: 114 N at 10.8° below +x.
b. Sam is at rest, so all the forces on him add to zero (S3.1). The ground's friction on his shoes is equal and opposite: 114 N at 10.8° above −x.
questions.finalAnswer: a. 114 N at 10.8° below +x. b. 114 N at 10.8° above −x.

steps.say: At rest, so the forces on Sam add to zero. The ground's force is equal and opposite to the leashes' net force.
